analysis.one_liner: Authorizes nearly $2 trillion over ten years to make public schools zero-carbon, hire more staff, and boost education funding.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in September 2023 and died there when the 118th Congress ended, despite 82 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would send roughly $1.9 trillion in federal money to public schools over ten years. It would pay to convert or rebuild school buildings as all-electric, zero-carbon facilities, fully covering the cost for the most vulnerable third of schools. It would also fund new school jobs — counselors, psychologists, nurses, teachers, and aides — with targets like one counselor per 250 students, and add roughly $44 billion a year for special education and $74 billion a year for schools serving low-income students. It was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in high-need and under-resourced schools, especially the most vulnerable third ranked by the CDC Social Vulnerability Index, plus Bureau of Indian Education schools. School workers would gain new positions, higher paraprofessional pay, and collective bargaining protections. Construction and retrofit workers would gain jobs requiring prevailing wages, apprenticeships, and local hiring. Taxpayers in high-poverty districts would benefit because federal money would replace local property-tax funding for building upgrades.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students, school staff, and construction workers

how_it_helps.text: Provides federal grants to convert existing schools or build new 'healthy zero-carbon' schools — all-electric, solar-equipped, free of asbestos and lead — with the federal share covering 100% of costs for the third of schools ranked most vulnerable, 2/3 for middle-ranked schools, and 1/3 for the least vulnerable.

Directs block grants to hire and retain educators and support staff in high-need schools for ten years, targeting student-to-staff ratios of 12:1 in K-8 and 15:1 in high school, one psychologist per 500 students, and one counselor and one social worker per 250 students, while raising paraprofessional pay and tuition support.
Authorizes $44 billion per year for Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) funding and $74 billion per year for Title I low-income school funding, for ten years each.

Requires contractors on funded projects to pay Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, use registered apprenticeships, sign project labor agreements on large projects, and avoid temporary staffing agencies, with preference for local hiring of veterans, formerly incarcerated people, and residents of the school's community.

Establishes a climate resiliency program funding electric school buses, backup power, green infrastructure, and high-speed internet so schools can serve as community shelters, with at least half of the funds going to environmental justice communities.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through new appropriations or borrowing — the bill authorizes its spending without any dedicated tax or offset, so the roughly $1.9 trillion would add to federal deficits unless separately funded. After ten years, local districts would have to keep paying for the newly created staff positions out of their own budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and, later, local districts

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $1.9 trillion over ten years — $446 billion for school buildings, $250 billion for staffing, $44 billion per year for IDEA, $74 billion per year for Title I, and $4 billion per year for resiliency — with no revenue source or spending offset attached.

Local districts must commit to permanently funding the new educator and staff positions after the 10-year grant period ends, creating a future cost obligation for school budgets that many districts would struggle to meet.

The bill layers extensive federal conditions on local schools — community-engaged plans, public dashboards, detailed hiring targets, and Buy American procurement rules — which would add administrative work and could slow or raise the cost of projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted: safer, cheaper-to-operate school buildings, more counselors and teachers, and finally-full funding for federal special education promises. But the scale is the problem. Nearly $2 trillion in new authorizations without any funding mechanism is far beyond what any Congress was prepared to enact, and the requirement that districts permanently absorb the new payroll costs after ten years would shift a large burden onto local property taxpayers. A smaller version would face the same design tradeoffs at a fraction of the fiscal risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the same day, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 28, 2023, by Rep. Jamaal Bowman and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
82 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list contains no Republicans.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral; the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of large new federal spending are better off, since the roughly $1.9 trillion in authorizations never advanced. Schools and the industries that would have benefited — construction, retrofit, and renewable energy — remain under the status quo, so no new money flowed anywhere; the cost of the bill's failure falls on students in high-need schools who would have gained counselors, nurses, and healthier buildings.

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and the Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 82 cosponsors.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no committee action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 82 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; with Republicans controlling the House and its Education Committee, the bill never advanced beyond referral.

industries.note: The bill would direct hundreds of billions of dollars into school building projects, with prevailing wages, project labor agreements on large jobs, and apprenticeship requirements steering work toward unionized contractors. The jobs and the healthier buildings would both serve the public.

All-electric schools with solar panels, batteries, and Buy American sourcing would create a large mandated market for heat pumps, solar, and electrical equipment made in the U.S. The public gets cleaner, cheaper-to-run schools from the same purchases.

The bill requires school heating, water heating, and cooking to be all-electric and keeps new schools 2,500 feet from oil and gas wells, displacing gas infrastructure in schools. Keeping gas systems in schools is worth less to these suppliers than it would cost the public in emissions and indoor air quality.

Contractors on funded projects could not hire workers through temporary staffing agencies except in certified short-term labor crunches, converting what would have been temp jobs into permanent positions with prevailing wages.
